conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood glucose was 54 when you arrived, and it dropped to 29 later. That’s very low and likely why you’re so weak and sleepy. We gave you some sugar, and you’re improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… so that’s why I feel so out of it? But my heart was racing too—was that from the low sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Low blood sugar can make your heart race. You were in atrial fibrillation with a fast rate—up to 170. That’s dangerous, especially with your heart history. We think it happened because you missed your diltiazem and digoxin that morning, and the low sugar triggered it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to take them… I was feeling off. But my heart’s okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart rate is back to normal—around 70 now. Your EKG showed some stress, and your troponin went up a little, but it’s likely from the fast heart rate, not a heart attack. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… what about my dialysis? I can’t keep stopping early because of the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re addressing that. You still have steal syndrome symptoms. We’re continuing the midodrine and digoxin before dialysis to help maintain your blood pressure and reduce the pain in your hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helped last time. But why does this keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The graft pulls blood away from your hand, especially when your blood pressure drops. We’re balancing your meds to prevent that. The ultrasound showed your graft is working, but the cephalic vein is clotted—that’s not helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing can be fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Surgery isn’t recommended. For now, we focus on managing symptoms with medication and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright… what about my shoulder and hip? I fell a while back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked. The left humerus fracture is healing well—no treatment needed. The pelvic X-ray showed no new fracture, just arthritis. Pain is likely from the old injury and movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a chest X-ray. You have moderate fluid in your lungs—pulmonary edema. That’s from fluid overload, common with kidney failure. Your dialysis today should help clear that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel short of breath sometimes, even with oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on 2 liters of oxygen. Your echo showed your right heart is strained from high lung pressure, but your left heart function is now normal—much better than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your ejection fraction improved to 60%. But we still need to manage your fluid carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my diabetes? I know my sugars have been all over the place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and that’s a big concern. You’ve had multiple low sugars. We’re changing your insulin—now 10 units of Lantus at bedtime instead of 28 in the morning. And we lowered your gabapentin because it can cause drowsiness and confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel foggy sometimes. Is that from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. With kidney disease, drugs like gabapentin build up. We’re giving you a lower dose, three times a week after dialysis, to stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most stay the same. You’ll keep midodrine before dialysis, diltiazem, digoxin, and your other heart and stomach meds. We added heparin shots to prevent clots while you’re less mobile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You need a few more days. We want to make sure your sugars stay stable, your heart rate stays controlled, and you complete a full dialysis without pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I’m more awake. My hand still feels cold, but no pain during dialysis last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your blood pressure held up well with the midodrine. Your labs are improving—creatinine down to 7.8, and no signs of infection. Blood cultures were negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your symptoms were from low sugar, fluid overload, and the heart rhythm issue. All manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Weight’s down from 76.5 kg to 70.6 kg—good fluid removal. Your strength is returning, though you’re still favoring your left side due to pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The hip still hurts when I move it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but no fracture. We’ll keep managing pain with acetaminophen and oxycodone as needed. Your PCP can reassess if it doesn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. We’re planning discharge tomorrow. You’ve had two full dialysis sessions without pain or low sugars. Your mental clarity is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Where am I going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To an extended care facility. You’ll get help with daily activities and continue close monitoring of your sugars and heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any final changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just the insulin and gabapentin changes we discussed. Take your Lantus at bedtime, and gabapentin after dialysis. Keep using CPAP and oxygen at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the midodrine before dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, three times a week. It’s helping prevent steal syndrome. Call us if your hand gets painful or cold during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to leave. Your labs are stable, you’re alert, and you’ve completed all treatments. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just—what should I watch for at the facility?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your blood sugar regularly. If it’s below 70, treat it. Watch for chest pain, shortness of breath, or swelling. And keep your follow-up with your nephrologist and cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Lee. You were brought in after feeling short of breath and dizzy during dialysis earlier today. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, doc. I was about three hours into dialysis when I started feeling weak and couldn’t catch my breath. My blood pressure dropped, and they said my left leg was hurting, so they sent me here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned leg pain—can you describe it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s that burning, tingling feeling I get in my feet, mostly. It’s worse today, but it’s been going on for years. My doctor says it’s from diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like diabetic neuropathy. We’ll keep you on your gabapentin and lidocaine patches for that. While you were in the ER, you also reported chest pressure, palpitations, and nausea—did that come on later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, after I got here. I got this heavy feeling in my chest, was sweating, and felt sick to my stomach. I was scared it was a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We took an EKG and checked your troponin levels—your heart rhythm is still atrial fibrillation, which you already have, but there’s no sign of a heart attack. Your troponins stayed stable at 0.4, which doesn’t indicate new damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t my heart? But why did I feel that way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to the low blood pressure you had during dialysis. When your pressure drops suddenly, it can cause symptoms like chest discomfort and nausea, especially with your heart condition. Your pressure is stable now in the 120s, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my lungs? I’ve been short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows mild pulmonary edema—some fluid in the lungs—but it’s not worse than before. That’s common with kidney disease and can get worse if you’re overloaded with fluid. But since you just had dialysis, this is likely stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my leg—could it be a blood clot? That’s what I was worried about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your left leg to check for a clot, and it came back negative. No DVT. The pain is most likely from your neuropathy, not a new clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. What about my heart rate? It’s been fast lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on diltiazem and digoxin, which help control your atrial fibrillation. Your heart rate was in the 120s earlier, but it’s come down to 75 now. That’s a good improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’ve monitored you overnight, and everything remains stable. Your blood pressure and heart rate are normal, and your symptoms have resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go back to the nursing home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to discharge you back to the extended care facility. You didn’t need dialysis here, so just continue your regular schedule—Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are my meds staying the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your medications are continuing as before—your insulin, digoxin, diltiazem, gabapentin, and others. We’ve added emergency hypoglycemia supplies like glucose gel and glucagon, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my chest pain—should I still use the nitroglycerin if it comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you have chest pain again, take one nitroglycerin tablet under your tongue and wait five minutes. If it doesn’t help, take another. But call your nurse or 911 if it persists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Anything else I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than three pounds in a day, let your doctor know—it could mean fluid buildup. And keep following up with your primary care doctor and transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks, doc. I’m glad it wasn’t my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. Have a good one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too, Mr. Johnson. The transport team will get you ready to leave soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You were brought in after not being able to finish your dialysis session today. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I started dialysis like normal, took a little nap, and when I woke up, I had this total body ache. It got worse fast, so bad I had to stop the treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the pain went away once the needles were removed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. As soon as they took the catheter out, the pain stopped. But I’ve been having this for months now—can’t even finish two hours of dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really tough. We know you’ve had issues with your left arm fistula before—steal syndrome—and they banded it recently. But the pain is still happening, even with the new catheter on the right side?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, same pain. I thought changing the access would help, but no luck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re going to run some tests—blood work and a chest X-ray—to make sure there’s no infection or fluid overload. But based on your history, this might be related to your fistula still pulling too much blood, even after banding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what can we do? I can’t keep living like this—can’t even finish dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering a procedure to permanently close off the fistula. That might stop the pain during dialysis. But we’ll need to discuss it with the transplant surgery team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, your labs came back. Your potassium was high at 6.9 when you arrived, but it’s come down to 5.2. Your kidney function is stable, and no signs of infection. The chest X-ray shows mild fluid in the lungs, but it’s not new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fluid might contribute, but your main issue seems to be the dialysis pain. The team agrees the fistula is likely still causing steal syndrome. Surgery has recommended ligating it—tying it off completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still be able to do dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll use the tunnelled catheter in your neck. It’s temporary, but it’ll work fine for now. The goal is to stop the pain so you can complete your treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll do it. I just want to get through dialysis without pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re scheduled for the fistula ligation today. The surgery team will tie off the blood flow in your left arm. It’s a short procedure under sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel anything. Afterward, there might be some soreness at the site, but we’ll manage that with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, the surgery went well. The fistula was successfully ligated. No complications. You’ll stay in recovery for a few hours, then return to your room.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s gone now? The fistula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, blood flow is completely stopped. You’ll use the catheter for dialysis going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re scheduled for a full dialysis session using the catheter. We’ll monitor you closely for any pain or issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. What if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful that removing the fistula’s pull will help. If you do feel pain, let us know right away. But so far, your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you completed the full 4.5-hour session with no pain. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel a thing. That’s the first time in months!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we hoped for. But I know you’ve still been having pain in your legs, back, and shoulders. It’s not from dialysis, but we want to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, that pain’s been there for years. Diabetes, they say. But the oxycodone isn’t helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted palliative care. They’re starting you on nortriptyline—it’s often helpful for nerve pain from diabetes. It may take a few weeks to work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try anything. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look stable. Creatinine is 6.9, potassium 4.1—good. You’ve had two full dialysis sessions without pain. We’re thinking about discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But what about my other pain? And my heart? I’m still not on blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right. Your atrial fibrillation puts you at risk for stroke, but because of your history of GI bleeds, we’re cautious about blood thinners. Your PCP will review that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve increased your oxycodone to 7.5 mg as needed and started nortriptyline at night. Palliative care will follow up with you as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health? I’ve been feeling down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your citalopram was increased to 40 mg daily. We know depression is tough with chronic illness. Keep talking to your providers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also recommend seeing neurology for your weakness and an eye specialist for your diabetes-related vision issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll make those appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your dialysis chair at the outpatient center. An extra soft cushion might help you tolerate longer sessions more comfortably.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good idea. I’ll ask them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge today. You’ve done two full dialysis sessions without pain, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So I go back to the extended care facility?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll continue dialysis through the catheter. The fistula is closed, so no more access issues there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take all your usual meds, plus nortriptyline at night and the higher-dose oxycodone as needed. Keep using insulin as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my weight goes up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than three pounds, call your doctor. That could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, doc. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your appointments, take your meds, and we’ll see you doing even better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. Just the usual aches, but I’ll try the new meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And remember—palliative care will call you next week to talk about pain and goals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be ready to talk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you to the extended care facility in about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge summary. Please review it with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in one last time. Still feeling okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Take care, Mr. ___. We’re glad we could help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Safe travels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—discharge complete.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: All good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel. You were brought in from your nursing facility because you're feeling fatigued and unwell. Can you tell me more about how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… just really tired. I missed dialysis yesterday—went to my nephew’s house for dinner. Woke up this morning feeling heavy, like I couldn’t catch my breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’re on hemodialysis three times a week, correct? Missing a session can build up fluid and potassium, which might explain how you’re feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, Tuesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays. I didn’t think missing one would hit me this hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, especially with your heart function. Your labs show high potassium—6.8—which is dangerous. We gave you insulin and sugar to bring it down, and you’ll get dialysis tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so weak? My legs feel like lead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. High potassium affects your muscles and heart. Dialysis will clean that out. Your chest X-ray also shows some fluid in your lungs—moderate pulmonary edema—so removing fluid will help your breathing too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I just don’t want to be stuck here long. I’m tired of all this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll get you dialyzed tomorrow, and if things go well, you could be back to your facility in a few days. But we need to make sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat potassium is down to 5.9—better, but still high. We’re scheduling dialysis for 10 a.m. today instead of tomorrow to get ahead of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? But dialysis always makes me ache all over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you’ve had pain with dialysis before. You were seen by palliative care last admission. We’ve asked them to consult again to help adjust your pain meds so you can tolerate treatment better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Last time they changed my meds, I was too sleepy. I don’t want to be out of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a fair concern. We’ll start with small changes and watch closely. The goal is comfort without oversedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished your dialysis session. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired… but my breathing feels easier. Less pressure in my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We removed about three liters of fluid. Your oxygen is now at 97% on room air, so we’re turning it off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium is now 5.2, and creatinine dropped to 8.9. You’re improving. But I noticed you seemed a bit drowsy last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I don’t remember much after 8 p.m. Was I sleeping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were very lethargic. We checked for infection—blood cultures are negative, no fever since a brief spike to 100.8. We think it’s from the pain meds, especially the oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pain meds made me out of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re sensitive to them. Palliative care is adjusting your regimen: switching to OxyContin 10mg in the morning only, and lower PRN doses. We’ll stop the nighttime dose for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I just want to feel clear-headed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a brief episode of fast heart rate yesterday—rate around 110. It slowed with a dose of diltiazem. Your oral dose is now increased to 240mg daily to prevent that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart races sometimes. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history of atrial fibrillation, fast rates can strain your heart. But we caught it early. You’re on digoxin too, which helps control the rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re due for dialysis again today. How’s your pain been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I’m not as achy. But I’ve been thinking… I’m tired of this cycle. I don’t know if I want to keep doing dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big decision. I want to make sure you’re making it with full support. We can talk more, and I’ll arrange for a social worker and nephrologist to speak with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just feel like I’m not living. I’m always sick, always in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. But today, you’re breathing better, your labs are improving, and your pain is more manageable. Maybe we can keep working on quality of life while continuing treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with dialysis. Your potassium is now 4.6—perfect. Creatinine is down to 7.1.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. We’re on track for you to go home—back to your facility—by the weekend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another chest X-ray yesterday. It shows improvement in the fluid in your lungs—no pneumonia. Blood cultures were negative, so no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about that fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was brief and likely not infectious. More likely due to your body being stressed from fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your blood sugar. You had a low reading—62—yesterday. Because you weren’t eating much, we reduced your insulin dose to 8 units at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been nauseous. Ondansetron helps a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring your intake. When you’re eating better, we may need to increase insulin again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking more alert today. Your labs this morning show potassium 4.3, creatinine 6.8. You’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Clearer in my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The change in pain meds helped. We’ll send you home with OxyContin 10mg in the morning and lower PRN doses. Hold them if you feel too sleepy or your breathing slows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep the gabapentin and nortriptyline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both continue. They help with nerve pain from diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged your discharge for tomorrow. You’ll return to your extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll keep doing dialysis… for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We’ll keep working with you to make it more tolerable. Please weigh yourself daily—call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go. Your final labs are stable, you’re breathing well, and you’re more alert.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll try to make better choices—no more missed dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. Keep in touch with your kidney team, and don’t hesitate to call if you feel unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thanks for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m okay. A little tired, but not like when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Remember your new pain meds—only take the PRN if needed, and stop if you feel too drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Morning pill, and small doses if I need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep taking your sevelamer with meals to control your phosphorus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t forget. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed, but hopefully not too soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. You’re all set to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in one last time. How’s the ride been so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smooth. I’m ready to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Remember to call if anything changes—especially weight gain, trouble breathing, or chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in because you were feeling confused and weak. Can you tell me how you're feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay now. I was just tired. They gave me something for pain this morning—oxycodone. I think that made me sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. You also had a short dialysis session yesterday. That, along with the pain medicine and a high level of digoxin in your blood, may have contributed to your confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Digoxin? I take that for my heart. But at the rehab, they were giving it every day, not every other day like at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s likely why your level was high—2.7, which is above the safe range. We’ve held the digoxin for now and will restart it at home on the every-other-day schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So that could’ve made me confused?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with your kidney function. Your kidneys clear digoxin slowly, so it builds up. We’ll check it again before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve been having more shoulder pain too. That’s why they gave me extra oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. But strong painkillers can make confusion worse, especially when combined with other things. We’re switching to acetaminophen and lidocaine patches to manage your pain more safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be in pain, but I don’t want to be out of it either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll balance it. Palliative care will help us keep your pain under control without sedation. You’ll keep your morning OxyContin and use low-dose oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a CT scan of your head to make sure there was no stroke or bleeding. It came back normal—no acute issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray showed mild fluid in the lungs, which we think is from missing part of your dialysis. We’ll get you dialyzed tomorrow to clear that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel short of breath though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it builds up slowly. Your body gets used to it. Dialysis will help remove the extra fluid and improve your breathing, even if you don’t feel it now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. When will I get dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow at noon. We’ve scheduled it. Your potassium was high—5.5—which also improves with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I missed dialysis, my potassium was high too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and this time, it went up to 6, but we caught it early. No heart rhythm issues, so that’s good. Dialysis will bring it down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll make sure not to miss dialysis again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are looking better. Your potassium is now 4.4, and creatinine dropped from 6.4 to 4.2 after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. Your mental clarity has improved too. You’re more alert today. The digoxin level is now 2.0—still a bit high but coming down. We’ll restart it at home every other day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I’ve been feeling a little flutter sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw some atrial flutter on the monitor, but your heart rate stayed low—around 50—likely due to the high digoxin. Now that it’s improving, we expect your rhythm to stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not on blood thinners because of past bleeding, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Because of your history of GI bleeds, we avoid Coumadin. But we’ll keep you on diltiazem to control your heart rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my calcium? I saw it was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your calcium is elevated—11.2. Your PTH level was high too, which suggests hyperparathyroidism. We’re starting cinacalcet to help control it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that related to my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. With ESRD, the parathyroid glands can become overactive. Cinacalcet helps lower PTH and calcium. We’ll monitor it over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my shoulder pain—should I get an X-ray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You already had one as an outpatient. It showed arthritis, no fracture. We’ll keep managing it with lidocaine patches and acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sad lately. It’s the anniversary of my brother’s passing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry to hear that. You’re on citalopram and nortriptyline, which help with both mood and nerve pain. We held mirtazapine for now because it can cause drowsiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I just want to feel clear and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today to the extended care facility. Your mental status is much improved, labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your digoxin every other day—never daily. Watch for nausea, dizziness, or vision changes, which could mean it’s too high. Keep using your pain meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on schedule. Any missed session can lead to fluid or potassium buildup. Also, avoid Fleet enemas—they contain phosphate, which your kidneys can’t handle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll remember that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your follow-up includes seeing neurology for weakness and palliative care for pain. Keep taking cinacalcet daily for your calcium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling clearer. The team will get your discharge papers ready, and you’ll be on your way soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure the rehab staff knows about the digoxin schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please do. We’ve also sent clear instructions to them. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the hospital because you were feeling very weak and lethargic, and you had an episode of vomiting. We’re trying to figure out what’s going on. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired… sleepy. Didn’t sleep last night. Not in pain though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’re very drowsy, which we’re concerned about. We did some blood tests and found your calcium level is quite high, and your digoxin level is also elevated. These could be contributing to your confusion and fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Digoxin? I take that for my heart… every other day like they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but in kidney disease, it can build up even with correct dosing. Your level is 2.6, which is too high. We’re going to stop it for now and talk to your cardiologist. We also found you’re very constipated, which might have caused the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… yeah, haven’t gone in days. But I had a bowel movement after I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ll keep an eye on that. Your calcium is 12.4, which is high. This can also make you sleepy and confused. We think it’s related to your kidney disease and possibly the vitamin D you get with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop digoxin, manage your calcium with medication adjustments, and continue your regular dialysis. We’ve increased your cinacalcet dose to help with calcium. We’ll also check for other causes like infection or heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan shows some fluid in your lungs, likely from mild heart failure or atelectasis. No bowel obstruction, but you do have some rectal wall thickening, possibly from constipation. Your bones show changes from kidney disease—osteosclerosis and some old lesions called brown tumors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Brown tumors? Is that cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not cancer. In kidney disease, high calcium and PTH can cause bone changes. Your PTH is elevated but stable, so it’s likely part of your chronic condition. Hematology looked at your blood proteins and said it’s not myeloma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your digoxin level is coming down, and your mental status is a bit better. We’re still seeing some crackles in your lungs. Your oxygen is 98% on 2 liters, but we’re watching for pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been coughing. Is that pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not clearly. Your chest X-ray shows some fluid and congestion, but no focal infection yet. We’ll keep monitoring. We started benzonatate for the cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a low-grade fever yesterday. We checked for C. diff and norovirus—both negative. Blood cultures are also negative. No sign of active infection so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little better. Still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your calcium is improving. We’re keeping cinacalcet at the higher dose. Your digoxin level dropped to 1.8—still coming down. We’ll repeat it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My face cyst is draining. It hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll apply warm compresses and keep it clean. If it doesn’t improve, we may need to drain it at the bedside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned testicular pain. We did an ultrasound. There’s a small 8mm area in your right testicle. It’s likely from old trauma, but we’ll follow up to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I sit on it sometimes in the wheelchair. Could that do it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chronic pressure could cause that. We don’t think it’s urgent, but we’ll monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mental status is more alert. You’re still sleepy, but you’re following conversations better. This was likely a mix of high calcium, digoxin, and poor nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want to eat more. Can I?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re cautious. You’ve had some coughing when eating. We’ll start with softer foods and thickened liquids to reduce aspiration risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You spiked a fever two days ago and had low oxygen. Your chest X-ray showed new infiltrates on the right. We started antibiotics—vancomycin and cefepime—for possible pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt short of breath. Is it from my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but the X-ray suggests infection. Your heart function has actually improved—EF is now 55%, up from 30%. But atrial fibrillation with fast rate can still happen, especially if you desaturate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The antibiotics are finishing today. Your fever is gone, and oxygen is back to room air. But we’re still concerned about swallowing. The speech team says you aspirate thin liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but I want to eat regular food. I know the risks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. We’ll advance your diet for comfort, but we need to warn you—eating could lead to more pneumonia or heart rhythm issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I accept that. I want to live as I choose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support your choice. We’ve updated your code status to DNR/DNI based on our discussion. Palliative care is helping with symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had another fever last week. We started a new antibiotic—ceftazidime—along with vancomycin. The X-ray showed worsening right lung infiltrate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tired of being sick. I just want to be comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re focusing on comfort now. You’re not on aggressive treatments. We’ll keep managing symptoms and infections as they come, but no ICU or intubation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows improvement in the right lung. We’re finishing the antibiotics. Your calcium and digoxin levels are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any chance I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed with your son. He wanted to take you in, but he can’t manage the care. So we’re looking at hospice or long-term care, but you’d prefer to eat and be comfortable here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve lived my life. Just keep me out of pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You desaturated suddenly last night. The X-ray shows worsening right pneumonia. We’re restarting vancomycin and cefepime for HCAP coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was eating… I know it’s risky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and each time you aspirate, it can trigger a rhythm problem or infection. But you understand and accept that. We’ll continue supporting your choice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infection is responding. Your oxygen is better. The X-ray shows less consolidation. We’re almost done with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a few more episodes of low oxygen after eating. Each time, your heart goes into afib with fast rate. It’s dangerous, but you’re choosing to continue eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. But food is one of the few things I enjoy now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your symptoms managed. Palliative is helping with comfort meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable for a while. Your labs are better. Calcium is down, digoxin is 1.5—safe now. But your overall condition is fragile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready for this to be over. I don’t want more tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t do more tests. We’ll keep you comfortable. If you get worse, we’ll use medications to ease breathing and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed abdominal pain and vomiting. The X-ray shows possible small bowel obstruction. We could place a tube or consider surgery, but that’s not what you want.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No tubes, no surgery. Just keep me comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make you NPO and start a Dilaudid drip for comfort. This is now comfort-focused care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very weak today. Your blood pressure is low, and you’re not eating. We’re continuing comfort care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you… for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray confirms small bowel obstruction. But we’re not intervening. We’re focused on keeping you pain-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very quiet today. We’re here with you. Your breathing is slow, but you’re not in distress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your family is here. We’re all supporting you through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re peaceful. We’re not doing anything to prolong this. You’re not suffering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson passed away peacefully overnight with family present. He was comfortable until the end.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll notify the family and begin discharge procedures for hospice care.
